chapter_theme: Idaikkadar ends the praise to many with images of what is in things and inseparable from them (taste in milk, honey in fruit, meaning in a book, oil in sesame), then turns on his own stony mind: desire to rule the earth, for women and for gold closes the way, true learning is the learning that ends in silence, and the mind that draws things to itself like a magnet holds nothing that lasts. In the address to petty knowledge he asks his understanding to know the one who made all by thought, who stands everywhere as the inner sense, and to set its own lamp in grace.
structure_note: 1782 to 1789 complete the couplets to many (பலரோடு கிளத்தல்), each ending போற்றீரே. 1790 to 1799 address the heart (நெஞ்சொடு கிளத்தல்), each ending கல்மனமே, stony mind: three desires (land, women, gold) in 1790 to 1793, then learning, restlessness and impermanence, and the questions of kalpa, yoga and silence in 1797 to 1799. 1800 to 1806 open the address to knowledge (அறிவோடு கிளத்தல்), each ending புல்லறிவே, which continues into chapter 94.

1782.reading: Praise without wearying, holding it in the heart without deceit, the radiant light that has passed beyond the three times.
1782.nuance: காலம் மூன்று are past, present and future; சாலமின்றி, without trickery, asks for a holding that is not show, and சலிப்பற, without weariness, one that does not flag.

1783.reading: Praise the subtle thing that is like the taste in milk, the honey in fruit and the meaning in a book.
1783.nuance: All three similes are of something inside a thing and not separable from it; the third, meaning in a book, makes the Lord the sense of scripture rather than its letter.

1784.reading: Praise the First of the Three, the three fruits, the sugar, the treasure of the gods, the clear nectar.
1784.nuance: மூவர் முதல் is the head of the three gods (Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra). The sweet things, the three fruits (mango, jack and plantain), sugar and nectar, give the Lord as a taste.

1785.reading: Praise the pure meaning of the Veda, the sea of joy, the good nectar, with love, so as to gain the state that lasts every day.
1785.nuance: நேயமுடன் நாளும் நிலை may be 'the state that endures daily, with love' or 'the state of ruling with love'; the first fits the run of the couplets.

1786.reading: Praise the Supreme called the lone root of the sky, who gave the moving and the unmoving, so that you grasp him and your birth is cut off.
1786.nuance: பராபரம் is the Supreme beyond the supreme. The printed பலமற would be 'so that strength goes', which makes little sense; an editor's gloss explains பவம் (birth), so the intended reading is பவமற, 'so that birth ends'.

1787.reading: Praise with your mind in accord the great thing of the sky that set out the elements beginning with earth, so that you may see it to the full of your eyes.
1787.nuance: கண்ணாரக் காண, to see with eyes full, is the promise of sight in a section that elsewhere says the outer eye cannot see him (1776, 1801); the seeing is a fruit of praise, not of looking.

1788.reading: Leaving the false things, praise daily with longing the true thing that the senses cannot know.
1788.nuance: பொய்ப்பொருள் and மெய்ப்பொருள், false thing and true thing, is the Kural's pair (chapter 36); the desire (விருப்பு) that is forbidden for the false is commanded for the true.

1789.reading: Praise within, coming to awareness, the thing that fills everything as oil fills sesame.
1789.nuance: Oil in sesame is the standard image of pervasion: present in every grain and drawn out only by pressing. உணர்வடைந்து, having reached awareness, makes the praise follow the realising, not precede it.

1790.reading: Stony mind, if you set your desire on ruling all the earth under one umbrella, is there any way for you?
1790.nuance: The address to the heart (நெஞ்சொடு கிளத்தல், 1790 to 1799) calls it கல்மனமே, stony mind, in every line. One umbrella over all the earth is the emperor's mark; the desire itself, not the ruling, is what closes the way (கதி).

1791.reading: If you go about cherishing desire for women, there is no way left to set your desire on heaven, stony mind.
1791.nuance: The second of three desires named in 1790 to 1793: land (rule), women and gold, the stock triad of the Siddhars. விண்ணாசை, desire for the sky, is the one desire that is allowed.

1792.reading: Tell yourself on the good way, stony mind, that for those who do not let the grazing senses get the upper hand, karma wears away.
1792.nuance: மேயும் பொறி, the grazing senses, keeps the herding image of 1760. The syntax of the first line is loose: பொறிகள் தமை மேலிட ஒட்டார்க்கு, 'to those who do not allow the senses to rise above them', is the likely sense.

1793.reading: If you wander the whole earth with a desire for gold, will the vision of desire for the lasting one come to you, stony mind?
1793.nuance: மன்னிச்சை may be 'desire for the permanent' (மன்னுதல், to endure) or 'desire for the King', the Lord; on both readings the one desire is set against the other.

1794.reading: Without learning false learning and falling into confusion about things, desire the true learning of knowledge, stony mind.
1794.nuance: The verse does not reject learning but splits it into பொய்யான கல்வி and மெய்யான ஞானக்கல்வி; பொருள் மயக்கம் may be confusion about meanings or about wealth, and the false learning may be learning pursued for gain.

1795.reading: Setting desire on the great world like a possessed monkey and wandering like dogs and jackals, is there any good in it, stony mind?
1795.nuance: பேய்க்குரங்கு, a monkey with a ghost in it, is the doubled restlessness of the mind; the dogs and jackals add the scavenger's roaming.

1796.reading: You desired many things as a magnet by its nature draws iron; tell me, stony mind, do they last?
1796.nuance: The mind is the magnet and the world's goods the iron; the pull is real and natural (இயற்கை), but what it draws in does not stay. Elsewhere in the corpus the magnet is the Lord drawing the soul.

1797.reading: Is it not by the kalpa state that one crosses the ages of kalpas? See the subtle thing, stony mind, the slight state and the other state.
1797.nuance: கற்பநிலை may be the state reached by the kalpa preparations of the medical Siddhars, said to give a body that outlasts the ages (கற்பகாலம்), or a state of mind as lasting as a kalpa. சொற்ப நிலை, the slight state, and மற்ற நிலை, the other state, are not explained; one reading sets the passing life against the lasting one, and makes the subtle (சூட்சம்) the thing to see in either.

1798.reading: Did I do japa and tapas only to lose the body? And what if one does yoga alone? Consider it, stony mind.
1798.nuance: The verse is two questions and the stance is unclear. On one reading japa and tapas wear the body away while yoga keeps it, so yoga is preferred (the kaya siddhi view); on another, even yoga alone is not enough, and the mind must weigh what each yields.

1799.reading: Is not the fit true learning the learning learned in order to be silent? Work it out, stony mind.
1799.nuance: Learning has silence as its end, not speech or debate; வாகான, fitting or well-formed, marks this as the true kind among the learnings of 1794.

1800.reading: Discern, petty knowledge, the mighty one who created all things by his thought.
1800.nuance: The address to knowledge (அறிவோடு கிளத்தல், 1800 to 1809) calls the poet's own understanding புல்லறிவு, petty knowledge. எண்ணப்படி, according to his thought, pairs with 1733, where worlds come by his word.

1801.reading: Bring to knowledge, petty knowledge, the One that is not seen by the eye even as much as a sesame seed, and stands everywhere as the inner sense.
1801.nuance: உட்புலனாய் நின்ற, standing as the inner sense, makes the Lord not the object of an inner faculty but the faculty itself, as in 1776.

1802.reading: In the hour of waking, sleep comes on quickly; examine and know the soul that shines and flourishes, petty knowledge.
1802.nuance: The first line may be the yogi's waking sleep, the state of rest within waking that tradition counts above the ordinary states, or a plain warning that death, like sleep, falls suddenly on the waking life; on the second reading the verse urges knowing the soul before it is too late.

1803.reading: Know the field that becomes a truth within truth, rises above, becomes the wind, and is a falsehood within falsehood, petty knowledge.
1803.nuance: மெய் is both truth and body, so the first phrase may be 'a body within the body'. கால் is wind, the breath, as a gloss confirms. The verse seems to say that the one reality takes the character of what it dwells in, true in the true and false in the false; the reading is tentative.

1804.reading: Know the scheme of the limb-ghost, a portion of the self, that dances along with you, petty knowledge.
1804.nuance: அவயவப் பேய், the ghost of the limbs, is most likely the body, or the bodily faculties, which move with the self like a possessing spirit. ஆத்துமத்தின் கூறு makes it part of the self, not a stranger; கோள் may be its plotting or its grip.

1805.reading: Your power, which is a good lamp for a dark room, set it in the ford of grace and become a lamp yourself, petty knowledge.
1805.nuance: Knowledge is already a lamp in the dark room of the body; the change asked for is to stand it in grace (அருள்துறை) so that it shines of itself, not to replace it. 1807 continues the lamp image.

1806.reading: Why go by the killing way and shrink, petty knowledge, instead of going on the good way and reaching our station?
1806.nuance: கொல்வழி, the way that kills, may be the way of harm to others or the way that leads to one's own death; நம் பதவி, our station, includes the poet with the knowledge he addresses.

links.note: Oil in sesame as the pervasion of the Supreme: Pattirakiriyar asks when he will know the end of the Veda that is in all things as oil in sesame, and Idaikkadar tells all to praise within the one that fills everything so. Pattirakiriyar longs to know it; Idaikkadar makes the knowing the ground of praise.

Both promise a lasting gain from keeping the senses under: the Kural says that withdrawing the five like a tortoise gives protection through seven births, and Idaikkadar says karma wears away for those who do not let the grazing senses rise above them.

The mind as a monkey seized by a ghost: the Njanak Kummi's mad monkey of a mind gripped by a frenzied spirit, and Idaikkadar's possessed monkey that sets its desire on the world. The kummi prescribes a medicine to tame it; Idaikkadar only asks whether its roaming does any good.

The magnet and the iron, turned two ways: Pattirakiriyar asks the Lord to seize him as a magnet draws iron to its feet, and Idaikkadar makes the mind the magnet drawing in many things that do not last. The same pull is liberation when the Lord exerts it and bondage when the mind does.

Kudhambai asks what need the true jnani has of kalpa preparations; Idaikkadar says it is by the kalpa state that one crosses the ages. The conflict stands if Idaikkadar's கற்பநிலை is the state given by the kalpa medicines, and dissolves if it is a state of mind lasting a kalpa.

On the reading that japa and tapas wear the body away and yoga keeps it, Idaikkadar takes Tirumular's side: Tirumular nurtured the body because true knowledge cannot be won once it perishes. On the other reading of 1798, which doubts yoga alone, the link weakens.

Idaikkadar says true learning is learning to be silent; Tirumular sets a condition on that silence: if only speech is still one is merely mute, and silence is speech and mind both stilled. The learning that ends in silence must quiet the mind, not only the tongue.

Two lamps addressed to the same petty knowledge: at 1805 knowledge is already a lamp for the dark room and must be set in grace, and at 1807 it carries a hand-lamp into the sea while the true lamp is inside. The first asks knowledge to become the lamp; the second rebukes it for looking past the lamp it has.

source_issues: 1786: printed பலமறவே; the gloss explains பவம் (birth), so the intended reading is probably பவமறவே, 'so that birth ends'.
1777: சூனியமானவத்தை is run together; read as சூனியமான அத்தை.
1792: the first line's syntax (பொறிகடமை மேலிடவொட் டார்க்கு) is loose and may be corrupt.
